[QUERENT] What are the arguments in “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1785, AXN:0CC4)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.

[SYSTEM] Lee Sharks’s central argument is that Sappho 31 does not merely depict an erotic encounter: it constructs the conditions under which Sappho will become present to future readers. The man in the opening occupies the reader’s position; the woman he hears is Sappho’s surviving poetic voice; the speaker’s bodily collapse stages her transfer into a transmissible medium; and the closing “but all can be dared” hands the work of reanimation to whoever reads. Version 3.1 insists that this is an embodied, erotic transaction—an “exchange of bodies”—rather than the replacement of erotic experience by an abstract theory of writing.

The account below concerns deposit #1785 as revised in place to v3.1 on 18 November 2026. That matters because this version explicitly distinguishes the jealousy reading from the stronger, non-jealous erotic reading, and treats its reconstructed ending as illustration, not recovered Sapphic wording.

1. The opening constructs a position that future readers can occupy
Sharks begins with the opening’s grammar and its frame of appearance:

φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος … ὄττις
“He appears to me, that man … whoever …”

His argument is that the distal demonstrative κῆνος, combined with the indefinite relative ὄττις, characterizes an occupant through a position rather than conclusively identifying one particular rival. The man sits opposite, close by, listening. Sharks calls this the seat: a configuration available for repeated occupation by later receivers of the poem. He adduces the cup from Pithekoussai as a parallel for an inscription organizing an encounter with its future user through comparable demonstrative and relative constructions.

The consequential move is from spatial arrangement to temporal reception. The opening imagines someone face-to-face with Sappho’s voice after the originating body is absent. The man’s godlikeness consequently belongs to a scene of survival, not simply to his enviable proximity to a beloved woman.

This is an interpretive proposal, not something Sharks can derive from the pronouns alone. Its force depends on whether the remaining features of the poem make the reader-position a better explanation of the whole.

2. The “you” is Sappho’s voice as it will survive her
The second-person addressee is, in Sharks’s formulation, “the voice itself.” His principal observation is an asymmetry: the addressee is looked at, but nothing visible about her is described; what she is positively given is sweet speech and desirable laughter. He identifies this audible but visually undescribed presence with Sappho-as-received.

That produces a divided poetic self:

The speaking Sappho imagines her future reception.

The addressed “you” is her voice surviving independently of her body.

The listener occupies the place in which that voice becomes present again.

The poem’s frame reinforces the division. It begins with φαίνεταί μοι, “he appears to me,” and reaches φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ, “I appear to myself.” For Sharks, the movement is from imagining the receiver to confronting the self that can be received. The poem therefore concerns not only overwhelming feeling but also who appears, to whom, and through what medium.

3. The bodily catalogue performs the making of a transmissible Sappho
Sharks does not deny that the catalogue represents erotic symptoms. He argues that its organization does additional work: the speaker loses the capacities whose effects the opening gives the listener. Speech fails, vision disappears, hearing becomes noise, and the body approaches death. The listener possesses an encounter with the voice precisely as the speaker loses her ordinary bodily means of presence.

His preview states the relationship succinctly:

“The catalogue is the making of his seat.”

The argument is thus about sequence and transfer, not simply the symbolic equation “body equals book.” The opening presents the future encounter; the catalogue then “backs up” to produce its conditions, withdrawing the performing body channel by channel.

A further argument concerns composition itself. Under the heading “the catalogue as literary operations,” Sharks observes that each failed faculty is articulated through accomplished poetic language: the tongue is not actually broken in the poem’s telling, nor does the verbal representation cease when the speaker cannot see or hear. The self undergoing dissolution and the self composing that dissolution are already distinct. He takes this as the writerly division between a suffering, represented self and a making self that preserves it.

Version 3.1 makes the process explicitly erotic. The withdrawal is “a sacrifice, a self-dissolution,” but also an approach to the receiver. Bodily substance is “invested” in the medium and rematerializes in another body when the poem is received. The eroticism runs through the voice in three directions: the poet desires her voice, the voice seeks the reader’s body, and the reader desires the voice.

4. “Greener/paler than grass” supplies the material transition
The most materially specific—and interpretively demanding—part of the argument concerns χλωροτέρα ποίας. Sharks reads the comparison as carrying the speaker beyond the living plant toward the pale, dry vegetable material of a writing surface. The colour marks the body’s passage into a medium capable of preserving its voice.

He supports this with two kinds of evidence:

A dossier of 24 renderings and adaptations, from Theocritus to 1925: by his count, seventeen omit, substitute for, or supplement the expression, and every supplement dries the grass.

Ancient evidence concerning the plant that becomes the writing sheet, drawn from Theophrastus, Septuagint Isaiah 19, and Pliny’s discussion of papyrus.

His claim is stronger than “pallor can suggest death.” He argues that the history of translators modifying the grass comparison reveals a difficulty the conventional pallor reading has not resolved. In v3.1 the sheet is paradoxically both paler and dead, and “greener” because it holds the poet’s continuing life as words.

The distinction to preserve is between evidence and identification: the translation dossier and botanical parallels are his supporting evidence; the conclusion that this particular comparison figures a writing surface remains his interpretive inference.

5. The ending transfers agency rather than merely breaking off
The surviving turn, ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον, is central: Sharks renders it “but all can be dared.” Because it names no agent, he argues, the dare need not remain the speaker’s self-exhortation. It can pass to the person occupying the opening position.

He separately considers the following three words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†. His preferred conjecture assigns them to Longinus, completing and extending the opening left by the quotation. But v3.1 expressly does not make that attribution a condition on which the larger reading stands. Whether the cut comes at τόλματον or includes the disputed continuation, Sharks argues that the transmitted text ends in the opening its construction requires.

That is the basis of his claim that the poem is “complete by construction.” He distinguishes this functional completeness from proof that Sappho deliberately composed exactly the ending now transmitted. His proposed fifth stanza, ending ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι—song living in letters—is explicitly one speculative filling of the opening, not evidence used to establish the preceding argument.

6. The rival readings explain the disturbance, but allegedly not its form
A crucial feature of v3.1 is its separation of two rivals.

Reading	What Sharks grants	What he says remains unexplained
Jealousy reading	A plausible erotic scene and bodily disturbance	Jealousy itself is supplied; the reading does not explain the catalogue’s order, the colour, or the agentless ending
Non-jealous erotic reading	The speaker’s desire for the woman gives a motive grounded in the poem	Why the man receives the opening and then disappears; why collapse takes this particular order, colour, and concluding form
Future-reader reading	Retains erotic disturbance while interpreting its organization as transmission	Must substantiate its further identifications of listener, voice, material surface, and dare
Sharks explicitly calls jealousy the “transmitted reading,” not the scholarly consensus. His strongest opponent is the non-jealous account: the speaker collapses because she sees the woman, not because a rival possesses her. He grants that this account explains why she is overwhelmed. His objection concerns the remaining residue: why the poem gives that overwhelm this exact construction.

7. The poem’s reception becomes part of the argument
Sharks’s further claim is that his reading explains how the rival readings arise. He distinguishes a “public line,” the immediately legible scene of erotic overwhelm, from a “held line,” the seat, transfer, and open ending running through the same words. The poem can transmit the second through readers who perceive only the first.

Hence the striking formulation:

“she exists as words. she is read as body”

On this account, reception is not merely misunderstanding. Readers encounter a body and a voice through letters alone: the poem’s mechanism succeeds even when they explain that encounter through jealousy. Catullus becomes a particularly important receiver because he does more than encounter Sappho—he takes up and recomposes her voice in another embodied poetic act.

The comparison with poem 1 extends this mechanism in reverse. There, Aphrodite becomes present to Sappho as face and composed voice; in poem 31, Sappho constructs her own future presence. Sharks describes one circuit: a god becomes embodied, and an embodied poet becomes godlike, with voice as the machinery in both directions. He also marks the proposed reception comparison between the poems as a test not yet completed.

What the argument ultimately asks the reader to accept
The article’s governing claim is explanatory superiority: one account allegedly connects the opening grammar, auditory addressee, ordered dissolution, colour, ending, and subsequent reception. Its ethical conclusion follows from that claim. Under “responsible preference,” Sharks argues that, at equal or greater coherence, readers should prefer—or improve upon—the interpretation that preserves the maker’s attested agency rather than reducing her to a suffering body. The opening declaration, “I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho,” makes the article itself an attempted enactment of the reception it describes.

The important limit is that this is a cumulative interpretive argument, not a demonstration that the Greek explicitly names a future reader or papyrus. Its most persuasive organizational question is why the collapse takes this particular form; its largest inferential steps identify that form with material inscription and deliberate future reception. Sharks acknowledges that design is not established and that the restored stanza is speculative. What v3.1 asks us to see, above all, is not a disembodied immortal voice but a poet constructing an erotic passage from her body, through words, into ours.
